newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW - GM - West tough but East Europe promising.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - GM - West tough but East Europe promising.

text.p: Europe can expect to see more car plant closures and job losses, while manufacturers will have to get used to tighter profit margins, General Motors Europe chairman Richard Donnelly said on Tuesday.
Donnelly stopped short of predicting bankruptcy among any of the big six European car makers, but he did say they would face a shake-out.
According to Donnelly, the industry was tough enough to weather any foreseable storms.

As European car manufacturers get used to forecasts of stagnant sales in western Europe up to and beyond 2000, Donnelly pointed to exciting prospects in central and eastern Europe, where there was a potential market of up to five million car sales a year over the next 20 years time.
Western Europe's car sales are expected to rise by five percent this year to 12.65 million, GM Europe says. But this compares with the glory days in 1991 when 13.5 million cars were sold.
In an interview at the Paris car show, Donnelly said overcapacity was the root of the problem.

"There's so much extra capacity, that's the fundemental thing. There's 16 million units of capacity and a 12-1/2 million market so obviously some companies have been really aggressive to try to keep some semblance of high utilisation in their plants," Donnelly said.
Carmakers need to crank up production as near to capacity as possible to keep costs down. They will cut prices ruthlessly to keep the production lines at maximum speed.
Car buyers have been seeing the benefits of this as prices are cut and salesmen try to outbid each other with free offers of previously expensive extras like air conditioning or navigation systems.
Donnelly said GM Europe, which sells Vauxhalls through its British subsidiary and Opels across Europe, had not led price wars, but had intervened when it saw a danger to its key markets.

"We've not led price cutting. That's not to say we haven't necessarily matched price cuts. Obviously there is substantial excess capacity out there. That is causing aggressive discounting I guess is the best way to say it. We're doing ok. Profits for the first six months were good, we're running the plants full," Donnelly said.
GM Europe, a wholly owned subsidiary of General Motors Corp, has said it earned first half net income of $604 million on revenues of $13.37 billion.
"I think margins are going to continue to get tighter and tighter, I don't know when that will get better. There's going to be a shakeout at some point in time."
But this shakeout needn't be terminal.

"This is a very resilient industry but those sitting on high excess capacity and therefore high fixed costs will adjust that somehow. They will shut down plants or transfer production. I'm not predicting doom and gloom. The industry will work out on a company by company basis how to resolve this."
But Donnelly was looking east for inspiration.
"Obviously when you look to central and eastern Europe you see great potential. We have to say there is three, four, five million units of potential out there in the next 15 to 20 years."
